newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka president faces first test in local polls.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka president faces first test in local polls.

text.p: Election fever has crept into Sri Lanka ahead of a deadline this week for political parties to enter local polls billed as President Chandrika Kumaratunga's first political test since coming to power in 1994.

Nominations for the polls, in seven of the country's nine provinces, will close on February 12. A tentative date for the elections is March 27, but this has not been finalised by the Election Commission.
But even before the start of official campaigning, thousands of party posters have adorned walls and billboards in Colombo.

"Usually local government elections are not this crucial to the main parties," said political analyst Dayan Jayatilake. "But the stakes and consequences of this one go far beyond that of the control over local bodies."

All eight parties in Kumaratunga's People's Alliance coalition are fielding candidates. The opposition include the United National Party (UNP), which lost to the coalition in 1994 after 17 years in power, and three leftist parties.
Seats for assemblies in 12 cities, 31 towns and 195 villages will be up for election. The size of the assemblies range from nine seats in remote villages to 53 in Colombo.
President Kumaratunga has postponed the polls three times, using emergency regulations relating to the government's 14-year war with the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE).
The LTTE are fighting for an independent homeland for minority Tamils in the north and east of this predominantly Sinhalese island nation.

The government earlier scrapped plans to hold elections in two provinces in the north and east after moderate Tamil parties said these provinces, mostly controlled by the LTTE, were not ready for a free and fair poll.

Analysts say Kumaratunga will regard a victory at the local polls as an endorsement of her controversial peace plan aimed at ending the war, estimated by the government to have killed more than 50,000 people.

"Though much of the election rhetoric will be on local issues like roads, water and garbage collection, it is perceived as a plebiscite on larger issues, mainly the peace plan," said a senior government source, who asked not to be named.
The peace plan, devolving wide-ranging powers to Tamils in a proposed new constitution, is currently being debated by a parliamentary select committee. It must be approved in a national referendum.
The UNP has yet to say where it stands on the proposed new constitution. Sinhalese hardliners have criticised it as rewarding the separatists.
The UNP controlled more than 75 percent of local government bodies before they were all dissolved last month.
It has accused the government of postponing the election in a bid to cover its unpopularity due to high inflation and an inability to defeat the LTTE.
"(The poll) would put to test the UNP claim that the government's popularity is at a considerably low ebb," said Jayatilake, also editor of the Lanka Guardian magazine.

"The government winning this election would send a message to the UNP. Then they would have less reason not to support the plan," said Mavai Senathiraja, an MP for the moderate Tamil United Liberation Front.
